topics.name: Haymarket Affair
topics.kicker: Bombing at an 1886 Chicago labor rally · Remembered every May Day
topics.briefing: Much of the world honors workers every May 1 because of what happened in Chicago in 1886. On May 4, as police moved in to break up a rally in Haymarket Square for an eight-hour workday, someone threw a bomb. Seven police officers and at least four other people died in the explosion and the gunfire that followed. Eight anarchists were convicted and four were executed, though no one ever proved who threw the bomb.
topics.answerHtml: Haymarket Affair (or Haymarket Square Riot or Haymarket Massacre; do not accept “Pullman Strike” or “Homestead Strike”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1893, Illinois governor John Peter Altgeld pardoned Samuel Fielden, Michael Schwab, and Oscar Neebe, three men who had been in prison since this event, declaring that their trial had been unfair. The pardons badly damaged Altgeld’s popularity.
tossups.r: Four other men had been executed for this event in 1887. For 10 points, name this 1886 bombing at a Chicago labor rally.

tossups.p: Mayor Carter Harrison listened to the speeches at the rally that ended in this event, decided the crowd was peaceful, and went home. Soon afterward, Samuel Fielden was finishing the last speech when police marched in and ordered the crowd to break up.
tossups.r: Moments later, a bomb exploded among the officers. For 10 points, name this violent end to a Chicago labor rally on May 4, 1886.

tossups.p: August Spies, one of the speakers at the rally that ended in this event, edited the German-language newspaper _Arbeiter-Zeitung_ [“AR-by-ter TSY-toong”]. The day before this event, Spies had watched police fire on strikers outside the McCormick reaper factory.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1886 Chicago incident in which a bomb was thrown at police, after which Spies and three other anarchists were executed.

tossups.p: A labor federation that later became the American Federation of Labor had set May 1, 1886, as the date by which a shorter workday should become standard, and strikes spread across the country that week. Two days later, police shot strikers at a Chicago reaper factory.
tossups.r: The next night, a bomb exploded among police at a protest rally. For 10 points, name this 1886 Chicago event, which is remembered every May Day.

tossups.p: In 1889, socialist parties meeting in Paris formed the Second International and called for workers’ demonstrations around the world on the anniversary of the nationwide strikes that came just before this event. Those demonstrations grew into a yearly holiday in many countries.
tossups.r: That holiday is May Day, or International Workers’ Day. For 10 points, name this 1886 incident in which a bomb was thrown at police in Chicago.

tossups.p: Public fear after this event badly hurt the Knights of Labor, even though its leader, Terence Powderly, had condemned the radicals involved. Many workers turned instead to Samuel Gompers’s American Federation of Labor, founded later that same year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this May 1886 Chicago incident in which someone threw a bomb at police officers breaking up a labor rally.

tossups.p: Albert Parsons, a Confederate army veteran who edited the anarchist newspaper _The Alarm_, fled Chicago after this event but walked into court on the first day of the trial to stand beside his fellow defendants. His wife, Lucy, later helped found the Industrial Workers of the World.
tossups.r: Parsons was one of four men executed in 1887 after this event. For 10 points, name this 1886 bombing at a Chicago labor rally.

tossups.p: Judge Joseph Gary refused to give separate trials to the eight men charged after this event, and he allowed jurors who admitted they were already prejudiced against the defendants. Seven of the eight men were sentenced to death.
tossups.r: Four of them were executed in 1887. For 10 points, name this 1886 incident in which a bomb was thrown at Chicago police during a rally for the eight-hour day.

tossups.p: Emma Goldman, who said this event inspired her to become an anarchist, is buried in Forest Park, Illinois, near a monument to the men convicted after it. Lucy Parsons, whose husband Albert was one of those men, is buried nearby.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1886 event in which a bomb exploded among Chicago police at a rally for the eight-hour workday.

tossups.p: In 1889, a statue of a police officer was put up near the site of this event to honor the officers who died there. Officer Mathias Degan was the first of those seven officers to die.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this May 1886 incident in which a bomb was thrown at police breaking up a Chicago labor rally.

tossups.p: Governor Richard Oglesby changed the death sentences of Samuel Fielden and Michael Schwab to life in prison the day before four other men were executed for this event. A fifth man sentenced to death, Louis Lingg, had died in his jail cell.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1886 incident in which a bomb was thrown at Chicago police during a labor rally in a public square.

tossups.p: Flyers printed in both English and German called workers to the meeting that ended in this event, held in a square on Randolph Street on a Tuesday evening. Much of the crowd had already gone home by the time police arrived.
tossups.r: During the last speech, police marched in, and someone threw a bomb. For 10 points, name this 1886 event in Chicago.

tossups.p: Oscar Neebe was sentenced to 15 years in prison while his seven co-defendants were sentenced to death in the trial after this event. Prosecutor Julius Grinnell never showed that any of the eight had thrown the bomb, arguing instead that their speeches and newspapers had encouraged the unknown bomber.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1886 incident at a Chicago labor rally that led to the execution of four anarchists.

tossups.p: Inspector John Bonfield led the column of police that marched in to break up the meeting that ended in this event. Seven officers and at least four other people died, many of them in the gunfire that followed an explosion, and the person who caused that explosion was never identified.
tossups.r: The meeting had been called to support the eight-hour workday. For 10 points, name this May 4, 1886, event in Chicago.

tossups.p: Speakers at the meeting that ended in this event stood on a wagon on Desplaines Street, and a sculpture of a speakers’ wagon was dedicated at that spot in 2004. August Spies, Albert Parsons, and Samuel Fielden all spoke that night.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1886 Chicago incident in which a bomb was thrown at police, an event remembered each May Day.

clues.t: A bomb was thrown at police breaking up a labor rally in Chicago on May 4, 1886
The rally supported the eight-hour workday
Eight anarchists were convicted, and four of them were executed in 1887
Remembered around the world every May 1, on May Day (International Workers’ Day)
The rally was called to protest police shooting strikers at the McCormick reaper factory the day before
Speaker August Spies edited the German-language newspaper _Arbeiter-Zeitung_; he was one of the four men executed
Albert Parsons, a Confederate veteran who edited _The Alarm_, gave himself up to stand trial and was executed
Illinois governor John Peter Altgeld pardoned the three imprisoned men in 1893, calling their trial unfair
The bomb thrower was never identified; prosecutors blamed the speeches and writings of the accused
Seven police officers and at least four other people died in the explosion and the gunfire after it
The backlash hurt the Knights of Labor, led by Terence Powderly, while Samuel Gompers’s AFL grew
In 1889, the Second International, meeting in Paris, called for worldwide workers’ demonstrations every May 1
Mayor Carter Harrison found the rally peaceful and went home; police marched in as Samuel Fielden gave the last speech
Inspector John Bonfield led the column of police that broke up the meeting
The Federation of Organized Trades and Labor Unions (later the AFL) set May 1, 1886, as the deadline for a shorter workday
Judge Joseph Gary refused separate trials and seated jurors who admitted they were prejudiced
Oscar Neebe got 15 years in prison; prosecutor Julius Grinnell won death sentences for the other seven
Governor Richard Oglesby changed the death sentences of Fielden and Michael Schwab to life; Louis Lingg died in his cell
Executed on November 11, 1887: August Spies, Albert Parsons, Adolph Fischer, and George Engel
Flyers in English and German called workers to the meeting near Randolph Street
Speakers stood on a wagon on Desplaines Street; a 2004 sculpture of a speakers’ wagon marks the spot
A monument to the convicted men stands in a cemetery in Forest Park, Illinois, near the graves of Emma Goldman and Lucy Parsons
Albert Parsons’s wife, Lucy Parsons, later helped found the Industrial Workers of the World (1905)
An 1889 statue honored the police who died; Officer Mathias Degan was the first of the seven to die

trap.title: Haymarket, Homestead, or Pullman?
trap.body: Three famous Gilded Age labor clashes get mixed up. The Haymarket Affair (1886, Chicago) began when a bomb was thrown at police during a rally for the eight-hour day; the Homestead Strike (1892, Pennsylvania) was a fight at one of Andrew Carnegie’s steel mills; and the Pullman Strike (1894) was a nationwide railroad boycott led by Eugene Debs. Governor John Peter Altgeld shows up in both Haymarket and Pullman questions, because he pardoned the Haymarket prisoners and later protested federal troops during the Pullman Strike.
trap.fix: Anarchists, a bomb, May Day, and August Spies mean Haymarket. Carnegie, Henry Clay Frick, and Pinkerton guards mean Homestead. Debs, sleeping cars, and Grover Cleveland’s troops mean Pullman. If Altgeld comes up, wait for the year: 1886 is Haymarket, 1894 is Pullman.
trap.line: Real answer line: Haymarket Affair (or Haymarket Square Riot or Haymarket Massacre; do not accept “Pullman Strike” or “Homestead Strike”)

topics.name: Helen Keller
topics.kicker: Author and activist who was deafblind · Learned language from Anne Sullivan
topics.briefing: When she was 19 months old, an illness left Helen Keller unable to see or hear. At age 6, her new teacher, Anne Sullivan, began spelling words into her hand, and at a water pump in Tuscumbia, Alabama, Helen suddenly understood that “w-a-t-e-r” meant the cool liquid pouring over her other hand. She went on to graduate from Radcliffe College, write books, and travel the world speaking up for people with disabilities.
topics.answerHtml: Helen Keller (or Helen Adams Keller; do not accept “Anne Sullivan”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This person’s mother read about Laura Bridgman’s education at Boston’s Perkins Institution in Charles Dickens’s travel book _American Notes_. A Baltimore eye doctor then sent the family to Alexander Graham Bell, who told them to write to the Perkins school.
tossups.r: Perkins sent Anne Sullivan to be her teacher. For 10 points, name this woman from Alabama who was deaf and blind.

tossups.p: In 1890, Sarah Fuller of Boston’s Horace Mann School for the Deaf began teaching this person to speak by letting her feel the position of Fuller’s tongue and lips. This person also learned to understand speech by touching a speaker’s lips and throat.
tossups.r: Her first teacher, Anne Sullivan, had taught her words by spelling them into her hand. For 10 points, name this author who was deaf and blind.

tossups.p: Mark Twain persuaded the oil executive Henry H. Rogers and his wife to pay for this person’s college education. In 1904, she graduated with honors from Radcliffe College, where she had written her autobiography, _The Story of My Life_.
tossups.r: She was the first person who was deaf and blind to earn a bachelor’s degree. For 10 points, name this student of Anne Sullivan.

tossups.p: Patty Duke won an Academy Award for playing this person, and Anne Bancroft won one for playing her teacher, in a 1962 film based on William Gibson’s play. Both actresses had played the same roles on Broadway.
tossups.r: In that film’s most famous scene, this girl finally understands the word “water.” For 10 points, name this woman whose childhood is shown in _The Miracle Worker_.

tossups.p: Michael Anagnos, the director of a Boston school for the blind, chose one of its recent graduates, a young woman with poor eyesight of her own, to travel to Alabama and teach this girl. That teacher arrived on March 3, 1887.
tossups.r: That teacher, Anne Sullivan, worked with her for nearly 50 years. For 10 points, name this woman who lost her sight and hearing as a baby.

tossups.p: In 2009, Alabama added a bronze statue of this person as a young girl to the National Statuary Hall Collection in the U.S. Capitol. Six years earlier, Alabama put her on its state quarter, the first U.S. circulating coin with writing in Braille.
tossups.r: The statue shows her at the water pump where she first understood a word. For 10 points, name this woman who was deaf and blind.

tossups.p: During a 1937 visit to Japan, this person was given an Akita puppy, often called the first Akita brought to the United States. She had been born in 1880 in Tuscumbia, Alabama.
tossups.r: An illness at 19 months had left her unable to see or hear. For 10 points, name this author whose teacher was Anne Sullivan.

tossups.p: This author dedicated her first book to Alexander Graham Bell, and a Harvard instructor named John Macy helped her edit it while she was still a college student. Macy married her teacher in 1905.
tossups.r: That 1903 book is _The Story of My Life_. For 10 points, name this woman who lost her sight and hearing as a baby.

tossups.p: This person joined the Socialist Party in 1909 and spoke out for women’s right to vote and for workers’ rights. In 1920, she was one of the founders of the American Civil Liberties Union.
tossups.r: She is best known for learning to communicate after losing her sight and hearing. For 10 points, name this activist from Tuscumbia, Alabama.

tossups.p: After this person’s teacher died in 1936, Polly Thomson, a Scottish woman who had worked with them since 1914, became her constant companion. This person died in 1968 at her home in Easton, Connecticut.
tossups.r: Her ashes were placed in Washington National Cathedral next to those of Anne Sullivan. For 10 points, name this author who was deaf and blind.

tossups.p: This person worked for the American Foundation for the Blind for more than 40 years, raising money and speaking around the world. In 1964, Lyndon Johnson awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
tossups.r: As a child, she understood her first word, “water,” while standing at a pump. For 10 points, name this student of Anne Sullivan.

tossups.p: This person played herself in _Deliverance_, a 1919 silent film about her life. In the 1920s, she and her teacher toured the vaudeville stage, where she answered questions from the audience.
tossups.r: Her teacher, Anne Sullivan, had arrived at her Alabama home in 1887. For 10 points, name this woman who was deaf and blind.

tossups.p: This author described how she sensed the world through touch and smell in the 1908 book _The World I Live In_. Nearly fifty years later, she published a biography called _Teacher_.
tossups.r: That book honored Anne Sullivan, who taught her to communicate after she lost her sight and hearing. For 10 points, name this author.

tossups.p: For decades, the town where this person was born has held a summer festival in her honor, and a play about her childhood has been performed outdoors at her birthplace, Ivy Green. Her father, Arthur, had been a captain in the Confederate army.
tossups.r: That play is _The Miracle Worker_. For 10 points, name this woman from Tuscumbia, Alabama, who lost her sight and hearing as a baby.

tossups.p: This author explained her faith in the ideas of the Swedish thinker Emanuel Swedenborg in her 1927 book _My Religion_. She also wrote essays supporting workers and socialism, collected in _Out of the Dark_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this author who lost her sight and hearing as a baby and learned to communicate with help from Anne Sullivan.

clues.t: An illness at 19 months old left her unable to see or hear
Her teacher, Anne Sullivan, taught her words by spelling them into her hand
Breakthrough at a water pump (1887): she understood that “w-a-t-e-r” spelled into her hand meant water
Her childhood is the subject of _The Miracle Worker_, a play and a 1962 film
Born in 1880 in Tuscumbia, Alabama
Graduated from Radcliffe College (1904), the first person who was deaf and blind to earn a bachelor’s degree
Wrote her autobiography, _The Story of My Life_ (1903), while still in college
Anne Sullivan came from the Perkins Institution for the Blind in Boston
Alexander Graham Bell advised her family to contact Perkins; she dedicated her first book to him
Worked for the American Foundation for the Blind for more than 40 years, raising money around the world
One of the founders of the American Civil Liberties Union (1920)
Received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from Lyndon Johnson (1964)
Shown on Alabama’s 2003 state quarter, the first U.S. circulating coin with Braille
In the 1962 film of William Gibson’s play, Patty Duke (as her) and Anne Bancroft (as Sullivan) both won Oscars
Mark Twain persuaded oil executive Henry H. Rogers to pay for her college education
Her mother read about Laura Bridgman, an earlier Perkins student who was deaf and blind, in Charles Dickens’s _American Notes_
Sarah Fuller of the Horace Mann School for the Deaf taught her to speak (1890); she understood speech by touching lips and throat
Perkins director Michael Anagnos chose Anne Sullivan, who arrived on March 3, 1887
John Macy, a Harvard instructor, helped edit _The Story of My Life_ and married Anne Sullivan (1905)
Joined the Socialist Party (1909), backed women’s suffrage, and wrote the essays collected in _Out of the Dark_
Polly Thomson, a Scottish aide, became her companion after Sullivan died in 1936
Died in 1968 in Easton, Connecticut; her ashes rest in Washington National Cathedral beside Sullivan’s
Alabama’s statue of her in the U.S. Capitol (2009) shows her as a girl at the water pump
Was given an Akita puppy in Japan in 1937, often called the first Akita in the United States
Played herself in the silent film _Deliverance_ (1919) and toured in vaudeville with Sullivan in the 1920s
Other books: _The World I Live In_ (1908), _My Religion_ (1927, on Emanuel Swedenborg’s ideas), and _Teacher_ (1955), about Sullivan
Her birthplace, Ivy Green, has hosted an outdoor performance of _The Miracle Worker_ each summer for decades

trap.title: Student or teacher?
trap.body: Anne Sullivan, the teacher who spelled “water” into Keller’s hand, is an answer line of her own, and many clues (the Perkins school, the water pump, _The Miracle Worker_) show up in tossups about both women. The title _The Miracle Worker_ actually describes Sullivan, not Keller. Laura Bridgman, who was also deaf and blind and was educated at Perkins about fifty years earlier, can also be a tempting wrong answer.
trap.fix: If the question asks for the person who lost her sight and hearing at 19 months, graduated from Radcliffe, or wrote _The Story of My Life_, say Keller. If it asks for the Perkins graduate who arrived in Alabama in 1887 to teach, say Anne Sullivan.
trap.line: Real answer line: Helen Keller (or Helen Adams Keller; do not accept “Anne Sullivan”)

topics.name: Henry Ford
topics.kicker: Carmaker who built the Model T · Made the moving assembly line famous
topics.briefing: Henry Ford didn’t invent the car, but he figured out how to make cars cheap enough for ordinary families to buy. His Model T, introduced in 1908, was soon built on a moving assembly line that cut the time to put together a car’s chassis from more than 12 hours to about an hour and a half. In 1914, he shocked the business world by roughly doubling his workers’ pay to $5 a day, and by 1927 his company had built about 15 million Model Ts.
topics.answerHtml: Henry Ford (prompt on Ford; do not accept “Gerald Ford” or “Ford Motor Company”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In Aldous Huxley’s novel _Brave New World_, people use this man’s name in place of God’s and count the years from the debut of his most famous product. Huxley’s characters even make the sign of a letter of the alphabet in his honor.
tossups.r: That letter, T, stands for his most famous car. For 10 points, name this carmaker who introduced the moving assembly line.

tossups.p: In 1915, this man chartered the ocean liner _Oscar II_ and sailed to Europe with a group of peace activists, hoping to end World War I by Christmas. Newspapers mocked the voyage, which became known as the “Peace Ship.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this industrialist whose low-priced Model T put millions of Americans behind the wheel.

tossups.p: With Woodrow Wilson’s encouragement, this man ran for the U.S. Senate from Michigan in 1918 as a Democrat and narrowly lost to Truman Newberry. He also bought the weekly newspaper the _Dearborn Independent_ and used it to publish antisemitic articles in the early 1920s.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Michigan industrialist who introduced the $5 workday in 1914.

tossups.p: After this man quit his second car company in 1902, his backers reorganized it under Henry Leland and renamed it Cadillac. A year earlier, this man had won fame by beating Alexander Winton in a car race at Grosse Pointe, Michigan.
tossups.r: In 1903, he founded the company that later built the Model T. For 10 points, name this automaker.

tossups.p: This man refused to pay for a license under George Selden’s patent on gasoline-powered cars, and in 1911 a federal appeals court ruled in his favor. Racer Barney Oldfield drove this man’s early race car, the “999,” to speed records.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this founder of a Detroit car company whose Model T first went on sale in 1908.

tossups.p: In a 1916 interview with the _Chicago Tribune_, this man declared that “history is more or less bunk.” Yet he later spent a fortune collecting historic buildings, including Thomas Edison’s laboratory and the Wright brothers’ bicycle shop, for an outdoor museum called Greenfield Village.
tossups.r: That museum stands in Dearborn, Michigan, near where he was born. For 10 points, name this carmaker who built the Model T.

tossups.p: This man said he got an idea from the overhead trolleys that Chicago meatpackers used to move sides of beef past workers. Using that idea, his Highland Park plant cut the time needed to put together a car’s chassis from more than 12 hours to about 90 minutes.
tossups.r: His factories then turned out Model Ts by the millions. For 10 points, name this industrialist who introduced the moving assembly line in 1913.

tossups.p: Inspectors from this man’s “Sociological Department” visited workers’ homes to check whether they lived the way he approved, which decided whether they received his full pay. In 1926, he gave his factory workers a five-day, 40-hour week.
tossups.r: That full pay was the $5 day he announced in 1914. For 10 points, name this founder of the company that built the Model T.

tossups.p: In the 1937 Battle of the Overpass, security men working for this man’s company beat Walter Reuther and other United Auto Workers organizers outside the River Rouge plant. His company did not sign a contract with the union until 1941.
tossups.r: His company had become famous for its moving assembly line. For 10 points, name this automaker who introduced the $5 workday.

tossups.p: In 1928, this man’s company began building a town in the Amazon rainforest of Brazil to grow rubber for tires, but the plantation failed. Closer to home, his River Rouge complex in Dearborn turned iron ore, coal, and other raw materials into finished cars.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American industrialist who introduced the Model T in 1908.

tossups.p: On October 21, 1929, the 50th anniversary of Edison’s light bulb, this man hosted Thomas Edison and President Herbert Hoover at the dedication of his museum in Dearborn. Years earlier, Edison had encouraged this man’s car experiments.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this carmaker, who built the Model T on a moving assembly line.

tossups.p: This man built his first car in a brick shed behind his Detroit home and had to knock out part of the wall to drive it out. That 1896 vehicle, which rolled on four bicycle wheels, was called the Quadricycle.
tossups.r: Twelve years later, he introduced the low-priced Model T. For 10 points, name this Michigan automaker.

tossups.p: The brothers John and Horace Dodge, early investors in this man’s company, sued him to force the company to pay larger dividends, and in 1919 the Michigan Supreme Court ruled in their favor. The Dodges had supplied engines and other parts for his first cars.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this founder of the car company that sold the Model T.

tossups.p: This man and his son Edsel created a foundation in 1936 that grew into one of the world’s largest charities. After Edsel died in 1943, this man ran his company again until his grandson took over in 1945.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Michigan industrialist whose company built the Model T on a moving assembly line.

tossups.p: In 1927, after building about 15 million of one model, this man shut down his factories for months to retool for its replacement, called the Model A. He had long resisted changing the older car.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this automaker whose “Tin Lizzie,” or Model T, came in “any color… so long as it is black.”

clues.t: Built the Model T (1908), nicknamed the “Tin Lizzie,” a car many ordinary families could buy
Introduced the moving assembly line (1913) at his Highland Park plant near Detroit
The $5 day (1914) roughly doubled his factory workers’ pay
Wrote that a buyer could have a Model T in “any color… so long as it is black”
Founded his car company in Detroit in 1903; it became one of the “Big Three” automakers
Built his first car, the Quadricycle (1896), in a brick shed behind his Detroit home
Worked as an engineer for the Edison Illuminating Company; Thomas Edison encouraged his car work and became a close friend
His River Rouge complex in Dearborn turned raw materials like iron ore and coal into finished cars
Created Greenfield Village, an outdoor museum of historic buildings such as Edison’s lab and the Wright brothers’ bicycle shop
Created a foundation with his son Edsel in 1936; it grew into one of the world’s largest charities
Replaced the Model T with the Model A in 1927, after building about 15 million Model Ts
His newspaper, the _Dearborn Independent_, published antisemitic articles in the early 1920s
In Aldous Huxley’s _Brave New World_, people use his name in place of God’s and count years from the Model T’s debut
Sent the “Peace Ship” (_Oscar II_) to Europe in 1915, hoping to end World War I
Ran for the U.S. Senate from Michigan as a Democrat in 1918 and narrowly lost to Truman Newberry
His second car company became Cadillac under Henry Leland after he left it (1902)
Beat Alexander Winton in a 1901 race at Grosse Pointe; Barney Oldfield drove his “999” race car
Won a court fight (1911) over George Selden’s patent on gasoline-powered cars
Told the _Chicago Tribune_ in 1916 that “history is more or less bunk”
Credited Chicago meatpackers’ overhead trolleys for the moving line, which cut chassis assembly from 12+ hours to about 90 minutes
His “Sociological Department” inspected workers’ homes to decide who earned the full $5 day
Gave his factory workers a five-day, 40-hour week (1926)
Battle of the Overpass (1937): his company’s security men beat United Auto Workers organizers, including Walter Reuther
Built a rubber-plantation town in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest (1928), but it failed
Dedicated his Dearborn museum on October 21, 1929, the light bulb’s 50th anniversary, with Edison and Herbert Hoover
John and Horace Dodge supplied parts, invested, and sued him; in 1919 a court ordered bigger dividends

trap.title: Which Ford?
trap.body: “Ford” can mean several different answers. Gerald Ford was the 38th president, Ford’s Theatre is where Abraham Lincoln was shot, and Ford Motor Company is the business Henry Ford founded in 1903. His son Edsel and his grandson Henry Ford II also ran the company. Saying just “Ford” earns a prompt here, and naming the company when the question asks for “this man” is wrong.
trap.fix: The Model T, the moving assembly line, the $5 day, River Rouge, Greenfield Village, and the Peace Ship mean Henry Ford. Watergate’s aftermath, the pardon of Richard Nixon, and the 1976 election mean Gerald Ford. Always say the full name, “Henry Ford.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Henry Ford (prompt on Ford; do not accept “Gerald Ford” or “Ford Motor Company”)

topics.name: Impeachment
topics.kicker: How Congress charges and tries officials · Can remove a president
topics.briefing: The Constitution gives Congress a way to remove a president, a judge, or another federal official for “Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors.” First the House of Representatives votes, by a simple majority, to impeach, which is like bringing formal charges. Then the Senate holds a trial, and it takes a two-thirds vote to convict and remove the official. Three presidents have been impeached, and the Senate acquitted all three.
topics.answerHtml: impeachment (accept word forms like impeach or impeached; prompt on removal from office)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: At the Constitutional Convention, George Mason proposed “maladministration” as a reason for this process, but James Madison objected that so vague a term would let the Senate remove a president whenever it pleased. Mason then substituted a different phrase.
tossups.r: The Constitution allows this process for “Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors.” For 10 points, name this process in which the House brings charges against a federal official.

tossups.p: The first federal official to face this process was Senator William Blount of Tennessee, who was accused in 1797 of plotting to help Britain seize Spanish Florida and Louisiana. The Senate expelled Blount and later dismissed the case, ruling that it lacked jurisdiction.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which the House of Representatives brings formal charges against an official.

tossups.p: In 1804, John Pickering, a federal judge from New Hampshire, became the first official removed from office through this process. Every official removed this way has been a federal judge, including Alcee Hastings, who was later elected to the House of Representatives.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which the House brings charges and the Senate holds a trial.

tossups.p: Vice President Aaron Burr presided over the Senate trial of Samuel Chase in 1805, only months after killing Alexander Hamilton in a duel. Chase is the only Supreme Court justice ever to go through this process, and the Senate acquitted him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, in which the House of Representatives can charge federal officials with “high crimes and misdemeanors.”

tossups.p: Secretary of War William Belknap rushed to resign in 1876 after he was caught taking money from a trading-post operator, but the House went ahead with this process against him anyway. The Senate acquitted Belknap, partly because some senators believed it could not try a former official.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that begins with a vote in the House of Representatives.

tossups.p: In 1868, the House used this process against a president who had tried to fire Secretary of War Edwin Stanton in violation of the Tenure of Office Act. Chief Justice Salmon Chase presided over the Senate trial, where Edmund Ross cast a key vote to acquit.
tossups.r: That president, Andrew Johnson, kept his job by a single vote. For 10 points, name this process in which the House brings charges and the Senate holds a trial.

tossups.p: In July 1974, the House Judiciary Committee, chaired by Peter Rodino, approved three articles accusing a president of obstruction of justice, abuse of power, and contempt of Congress. That president resigned on August 9, before the full House could vote on those articles.
tossups.r: That president was Richard Nixon. For 10 points, name this process, which the House of Representatives can start against a federal official.

tossups.p: Chief Justice William Rehnquist presided over a 1999 Senate trial that followed the House’s approval of charges of perjury and obstruction of justice in December 1998. Henry Hyde led the House managers who argued the case.
tossups.r: The Senate acquitted President Bill Clinton. For 10 points, name this process in which the House brings formal charges against an official.

tossups.p: In December 2019, the House approved two charges against a president, and Chief Justice John Roberts presided over his Senate trial in early 2020. In January 2021, the House charged the same man again, and Senator Patrick Leahy presided over the second trial because the man had left office by then.
tossups.r: The Senate acquitted Donald Trump both times. For 10 points, name this process, which the House has used against three presidents.

tossups.p: In Britain, Edmund Burke led this kind of case against Warren Hastings, the former governor-general of Bengal, in a trial that dragged on for seven years before Hastings was acquitted in 1795. George Mason mentioned Hastings’s case while the U.S. Constitution was being written.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that the U.S. House of Representatives uses to bring charges against officials.

tossups.p: In _Nixon v. United States_, the Supreme Court ruled in 1993 that the Senate may decide for itself how to run trials in this process, after a judge named Walter Nixon complained that a Senate committee, not the full Senate, had heard the evidence against him.
tossups.r: That judge’s removal stood. For 10 points, name this process in which the House brings charges and a two-thirds vote of the Senate can remove an official.

tossups.p: In Federalist No. 65, Alexander Hamilton explained why the Senate, rather than the Supreme Court, should hold trials in this process. The Constitution says that the president’s pardon power does not apply to cases of this kind, and that such cases are not tried by a jury.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that begins when the House of Representatives approves charges called articles.

tossups.p: In 1843, Whig congressman John Minor Botts introduced the first resolution aimed at starting this process against a president, John Tyler, but the House voted it down. In 1970, Gerald Ford led an effort to use this process against Justice William O. Douglas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which the House brings charges that the Senate then tries.

tossups.p: The Constitution limits the punishment in this process to removal from office and a ban on holding federal office again, though the official can still face a criminal trial in court. In 2010, the Senate removed Judge Thomas Porteous and also barred him from future office.
tossups.r: A two-thirds vote of the Senate is needed to convict. For 10 points, name this process that starts in the House of Representatives.

tossups.p: Members of the House known as “managers” act as prosecutors when the Senate holds a trial in this process, and senators take a special oath before hearing the evidence. The House Judiciary Committee usually drafts the charges, which are called articles.
tossups.r: A simple majority of the House can approve those articles. For 10 points, name this process, which can lead to an official’s removal from office.

trap.title: Charged is not removed
trap.body: Being impeached means the House has approved charges; it does not mean the official was removed. Andrew Johnson, Bill Clinton, and Donald Trump were all impeached, and the Senate acquitted every one of them. Richard Nixon was never impeached: he resigned in 1974 before the full House voted. Players also confuse impeachment with censure (a vote that formally scolds someone), recall (an election that removes a state or local official), and the 25th Amendment (replacing a president who cannot do the job).
trap.fix: If the question describes the House bringing charges and the Senate holding a trial, say “impeachment.” If it asks which president resigned, the answer is Nixon; if it asks for the first president impeached, the answer is Andrew Johnson.
trap.line: Real answer line: impeachment (accept word forms like impeach or impeached; prompt on removal from office)
